narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 18, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as a major risk for bar exam success.

Your first-year law school grades came next in importance and worked in your favor. Placing in the 7th decile outperformed the average of 6th decile among accepted students, giving the model some confidence that you could handle the academic demands.

Your undergraduate GPA ranked third and pulled the prediction back toward failure. A 2.7 GPA is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted students, reinforcing the model’s concern about your readiness.

Taken together, the very low LSAT score outweighed the positive signal from your first-year performance and the moderate drag from your college grades, producing an overall outlook of likely bar exam failure.

What you should do next is retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score. A strong improvement there would likely change the model’s assessment and improve your chances of admission.
